content.content:
The registry removal is the commit point of a discard, and it is taken only after every named draft's change act, workspace act and directory act have completed. Until a record leaves the store the discard has committed nothing: ending an open draft is the one change a discard makes, and it is made in the registry alone (tvxspkyy, twpvqstu). So the removal is not the first thing a discard does but the last, standing behind all the work the call performs on the drafts it names — behind the act that gives up the change each draft's workspace holds, behind the forget of each draft's workspace through the seam, and behind the removal of the directory each record's handle derives (vzposmvm, kxyznwxu). The three acts are named as the work that must lie behind the commit, not restated: the workspace act forgets the workspace and the directory act removes the tree at the derived path, in that order (vzposmvm); the change act gives up the change the draft's workspace holds, and what it does is a commitment of its own (kxyznwxu); where the change act falls among the other two is that commitment's to say, and is not settled here. Every named draft counts, because the invocation names one open draft per handle (kxyznwxu, lnpnkvkv): no named draft's record leaves before all of them have had the three acts completed. That the removal lies after all three acts, for all named drafts, is this node's answer; no prerequisite orders the removal against the work.

A failure at any point before that commit refuses the invocation. Any of the three acts can fail, and so can the removal itself while no record has yet left the store, and a failure at any of those points is a failure before the commit: the invocation is answered with a refusal and with nothing else. An absence at a workspace crossing is not such a failure — a draft whose workspace or directory is already gone is carried through as the same discard (vzposmvm), so those acts complete, the removal is still reached, and a drifted draft is discarded rather than refused (tvxspkyy). The answer is the invocation's and not one draft's, because one invocation answers once (kxyznwxu, lnpnkvkv): a failure on one named draft is not that draft's refusal standing beside another draft's success. That the answer to a failure before the commit is a refusal is this node's own; what a refusal says, where it writes and what it exits with are not, because how a failure of an act or of the removal reaches the user is left outside the workspace half (vzposmvm) and outside the verb surface (kxyznwxu), and is not settled here.

A failure before that commit removes no record, so every named draft's record stays at its handle. Because the removal is the commit, a failure before it leaves the store as it stood: the document of every named draft is still at `.deccy/work/<handle>.json`, every other record is still where it was, no record has turned from `open` to `landed`, and every named draft is still an open draft the registry holds (yomurusp, twpvqstu, vkkwusty). That outcome covers the whole subject set and not one draft at a time: no named record begins to leave while any named draft's work is still to run, since the invocation answers once (kxyznwxu) and every removal is behind the same commit. The refusal removes nothing; it does not reach back to unmake an act that already completed, since this node fixes what the store holds after a failure and not an order of undo, and a draft whose earlier acts completed while its record remains is still an open draft whose end is another invocation's business (tvxspkyy, vzposmvm). A failure that happens after a record has left the store is not this limb's case — the commit has been made — and what the store then holds is the registry write's own behaviour, its partial-write, atomicity and durability handling lying outside the removal as recorded (twpvqstu, yomurusp) and outside this node.

These clauses are one commitment, not three rules about different things. Take the commit point away and the removal is one step among four, free to be taken before the workspace, the directory or the change is given up, which would leave a named draft's record gone while the workspace that refers to it still stands and the change it held is still held. Take the refusal away and a failure leaves the invocation neither answered nor committed, with the work half done and no answer given at all. Take the no-removal outcome away and the refusal becomes a report about work that went through, the records of named drafts gone while the call was refused, so the store would disagree with the answer the caller received. The three hold one point together: the removal is last, so a failure before it is a failure of the whole call, and a failure of the whole call leaves every record at its handle.

What is not settled here is everything the commit point does not need. The verb surface — the command, its name and arguments — is the invocation's (kxyznwxu); the output, refusal wording, stream and exit status of a discard and of a refusal, including how a failure of an act or of the removal reaches the user, are left outside the invocation (kxyznwxu) and outside the workspace half (vzposmvm), and are not settled here. The exact jj invocation and flags behind the workspace act are the seam's (vzposmvm). The mechanism, atomicity, durability and concurrent-writer behaviour of the registry removal are left outside the store's commitment (twpvqstu, yomurusp). How the change the draft's workspace holds is abandoned belongs to the change act's own commitment (kxyznwxu). The record's field set and serialization are a separate commitment, left outside the store's removal (twpvqstu). This node answers one question — where the commit sits, and what a failure before it leaves standing — and answers it without reaching any of them.
content.rationale:
This decision is prose because the commitment is a policy about where a discard commits and what a failure before that point leaves standing — a relation among acts, not a single required behaviour of the CLI and not a stored artifact. Every edge is read rather than run: the clauses are checked against the recorded nodes, and nothing in the node needs a probe.

The commit point is this node's own answer and is written as such, while everything around it is grounded and attributed. The end of an open draft without landing, and the absence that follows it, are tvxspkyy's and vkkwusty's; the one document at the path the handle gives, the retention of every other record and the removal confined to the open end are yomurusp's and twpvqstu's; the workspace act, the directory act, their order and the tolerance of an absence at either point are vzposmvm's; and the invocation, one open draft per handle, the whole-call answer and the one answer per invocation are kxyznwxu's and lnpnkvkv's. None of them orders the removal against the acts. vzposmvm says so expressly, leaving how a failure of the seam or of the removal reaches the user outside itself; the store's removal fixes what it takes out and what stays, not when it is taken; and lnpnkvkv's whole-invocation refusal turns on a handle that names no open record, not on an act that failed. The order, the refusal of a failure before the commit, and the no-removal outcome are therefore stated here as this node's answer, and attributing any of them to a prerequisite would overstate that prerequisite's scope.

The three limbs are one point seen from three sides. The removal is the only change a discard makes (tvxspkyy, twpvqstu), so it is the point at which the call can be said to have happened; being the end of the work, it is reachable only after the change, workspace and directory acts have completed (vzposmvm, kxyznwxu); a failure before it is therefore a failure of the whole call, and since the call answers once (kxyznwxu, lnpnkvkv) that answer is a refusal; and because the two states of a record admit no third and retention keeps every record not removed at the open end (vkkwusty, twpvqstu, yomurusp), a refusal that has removed nothing leaves every named record at its handle, still open. Removing one record while a later act failed would split that single answer into two, which the subject set does not allow.

Two boundaries are drawn deliberately rather than overlooked. An absence at a workspace crossing is not a failure, because vzposmvm carries it through as the same discard; the refusal is about an act that does not complete, not about a draft whose workspace is already gone, which is why the content has a drifted draft discarded rather than refused (tvxspkyy, vzposmvm). And a failure that happens once a record has left the store lies after the commit; the content says so and leaves what the store then holds to the registry write's own behaviour, whose atomicity, partial-write and durability handling twpvqstu and yomurusp already leave outside themselves. The change act is named because the commit stands behind it, and nothing about it is settled here; its content and its place among the other two acts belong to its own commitment (kxyznwxu).

Not here, because the commit point does not need them: the verb surface and its output, refusal wording, stream and exit status, including how a failure reaches the user; the exact jj invocation and flags behind the workspace act; the registry removal's mechanism, atomicity, durability and concurrent-writer behaviour; how the change the draft's workspace holds is abandoned; and the record's field set and serialization. Each can be decided, changed or dropped without moving where the commit sits or what a failure before it leaves, and each belongs to a commitment recorded or planned elsewhere.
